title: What can and cannot mate

card.idea: Some material can force mate and some cannot, no matter how well you play it. A queen or a rook mates a bare king. A lone bishop or a lone knight never does, and neither do two knights. Knowing which is which tells you when to trade down and when to refuse.
card.habit: Activate the king and attack pawns in the endgame.

explain.text: Four pieces, one bare king. With the queen it is mate in a few moves. With the rook it takes longer but it is certain. With the bishop alone, or the knight alone, it cannot be done at all — you can chase the king forever and never mate him.

King and bishop against a bare king is a draw. The bishop covers one colour only, so the corner squares of the other colour can never be taken away. There is no move order that works, which is why this position is drawn before either side has played.

Two knights cannot force it either. You can build a mating net, but the moment it closes the black king has no legal move and it is stalemate instead. Only a mistake by the defender turns this into a win, and you cannot count on one.

challenges.prompt: Tap every white piece that could force mate on its own, with only the king to help it.

hints.text: Two of the four can cover a whole rank or file by themselves.

challenges.reason: The queen on b1 and the rook on c1. Both can cut the board in half along a rank, and that is what drives a king to the edge.

challenges.prompt: Now tap every white piece that could never force mate, however long you played.

hints.text: Neither of these two can attack every square on the board.

challenges.reason: The bishop on d1 and the knight on e1. A bishop only ever touches one colour, and a single knight cannot take the last squares away in time.

challenges.prompt: The white king already holds g7 and h7. Tap the square where the rook delivers mate in one.
challenges.reason: Ra8 is mate. The rook takes the whole eighth rank, and the king on g6 covers both squares on the seventh that Black would run to.

challenges.prompt: White has a king and a bishop. Black has a bare king. What is the result with best play?
options: A draw. A lone bishop can never force mate.
White mates, but it takes about thirty moves.
White mates only if the black king goes to a dark square.

hints.text: Count the colours the bishop can reach. It is one of the two.

challenges.reason: Drawn, and drawn immediately. The bishop touches one colour only, so half the board is permanently out of its reach and the king always has somewhere to stand.

challenges.prompt: Two knights against a bare king. What is the honest verdict?
options: It cannot be forced. Closing the net gives stalemate instead of mate.
It is a straightforward mate, easier than king and rook.
It is mate only if the knights stand on the same colour.

hints.text: Think about what happens on the move the net finally closes.

challenges.reason: It cannot be forced. The last square always comes off at the wrong moment and the game ends in stalemate. Treat two knights against a bare king as a draw.

challenges.prompt: White swings the bishop to h7, right beside the black king. Is it safe there?
reasons: Yes. The black king cannot reach h7 from h8.
No. The white king on e1 is too far away to matter.
No. The king on h8 simply takes it.

hints.text: h7 is next door to h8, and nothing of White's defends it.

challenges.reason: Kxh7 and the board is bare. A lone bishop has no helper, so putting it beside the enemy king just loses it — one more reason this ending is a draw.

challenges.prompt: You have nothing but a king against a king and a bishop. Survive eight moves. It cannot be done to you.

hints.text: Just walk. There is no net to step into, because a bishop cannot build one.

challenges.reason: No sequence of bishop moves mates a bare king, so any legal shuffling holds. Recognising this saves you from resigning a position that is already a draw.

takeaway: Queen or rook mates a bare king. A lone bishop, a lone knight and two knights never do — those endings are drawn before you start.
